b: What remains the most popular event in the chess calendar, particularly among mainstream audiences, got under way on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva. The elegant setting is particularly fitting for an event with such a rich history, especially at a time when efforts to popularise the royal game increasingly revolve around fast-paced competitions, often played online or on computers in front of a live audience.

It has been 140 years since Wilhelm Steinitz became the first officially recognised world chess champion, in 1886, and the tradition lives on. Eighteen players have held the undisputed world title, with Gukesh Dommaraju, the defending champion in Geneva, the latest addition to the list. Coincidentally, Gukesh was 18 years old when he defeated Ding Liren to become the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history.

Gukesh now faces Javokhir Sindarov in what is, by average age, the youngest World Championship match in history, with both contenders aged 20. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the day on which game 12 is scheduled to take place. Theoretically, the Uzbek grandmaster could claim the world title on his birthday, much as Magnus Carlsen did in 2016. The Norwegian secured his third victory in a match for the crown by defeating Sergey Karjakin in rapid tiebreaks on 30 November, the day he turned 26.
The first game of the match is under way at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny | Photo: Michal Walusza
Three chess legends commentating on the game - Peter Svidler, Vishy Anand and Peter Leko | Photo: Michal Walusza

As determined by the drawing of colours at Sunday's opening ceremony, Sindarov had the white pieces in the first game of the match. Following 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5, Gukesh opted for the Berlin Defence with 3...Nf6, and Sindarov agreed to allow the much-explored Berlin Endgame by playing 4.0-0 instead of opting for the Anti-Berlin with 4.d3. Gukesh followed the main line, and the theoretical battle began.

The Berlin has a notable history in World Championship matches. Vladimir Kramnik famously employed the system to neutralise Garry Kasparov's formidable opening preparation in their 2000 match in London. Fourteen years later, in Sochi, Magnus Carlsen secured his second world title with a victory over Vishy Anand in game 11 of their match out of a Berlin. The Indian legend incorrectly sacrificed an exchange to obtain a passed pawn on the queenside.

In Geneva, Sindarov blitzed out his preparation up to and including 13.Ne4, a novelty. Gukesh had already been playing at a more measured pace, and after spending over 15 minutes on his response to the new move, found himself 25 minutes behind on the clock.

A tense battle ensued, with Sindarov looking for ways to increase the pressure and Gukesh carefully dealing with the threats to maintain the balance. By the time Sindarov played 21.g4, a move that was not the engines' first choice, the Uzbek had a 30-minute advantage on the clock. Gukesh had just 16 minutes to make 20 more moves, with no increments until after the first time control.

The tension continued to build, as tactical complications were becoming increasingly difficult to avoid. Sindarov soon sacrificed a pawn temporarily, and precise play was required from Gukesh to keep the position under control.

It was at this point that the Indian star demonstrated that the time he had invested earlier in the game had been well spent. Gukesh began to play quickly and confidently, clearly having worked out the critical lines in advance. Despite the considerable disparity on the clock, the defending champion gave his opponent little opportunity to make progress.
Sindarov eventually saw no benefit in playing on, and the game ended in a draw by threefold repetition on move 38.
Javokhir Sindarov incorrectly claimed a draw and was penalised by the arbiters (he lost two minutes on the clock) - but that was just a formality | Photo: Michal Walusza

At the post-game press conference, Gukesh explained that he felt he had things under control throughout the encounter and did not "really need to be worried". Sindarov, for his part, acknowledged that his opponent had "defended very well".

Incredible first game of World Championship match! High quality game from both! Gukesh found great moves under pressure!
